questions.q: For a state with P(0) = 0.25 and P(1) = 0.75, measured over N = 1000 shots, what are the exact expected counts?
options: 25 and 75
questions.explain: Expected count = N * probability, so 1000 * 0.25 = 250 and 1000 * 0.75 = 750.

questions.q: Why does the lesson draw a clear distinction between 'expected counts' and 'one actual simulated run's counts'?
options: Expected counts (N * probability) are an exact theoretical average, while any single real run will typically differ slightly due to unavoidable statistical noise, so the lab only computes and plots the former
There is no real distinction; the two terms describe the exact same number in all cases
Actual run counts are always exactly double the expected counts
Expected counts only apply to single-qubit states, never to multi-qubit states
questions.explain: N * probability is an exact arithmetic expectation (a long-run average), while a specific real or simulated run will fluctuate around it from statistical noise -- which is why the lab avoids fabricating a specific 'actual run' number.

questions.q: In the bar chart code, what is the key difference in what the y-axis represents compared to the probability-distribution lesson's bar charts?
options: The y-axis here represents a raw count of shots (an integer, e.g. 250 or 750) rather than a probability fraction between 0 and 1
There is no difference; both plots always show values between 0 and 1
The y-axis here is logarithmic by default, while the probability lesson's y-axis is linear
The y-axis here represents time elapsed during the experiment
questions.explain: This lesson's bars represent expected shot counts (N * probability, e.g. 250 and 750 out of 1000), a count, whereas the earlier lesson's bars represented raw probabilities between 0 and 1.

questions.q: What does `ax.axhline(N / 2, color="gray", linestyle="--")` add to the plot, and why is it still informative even though this particular state is not an even split?
options: It draws a horizontal reference line at the 'even split' count value, which is informative here precisely because the actual bars (250 and 750) visibly sit on either side of it, highlighting the skew
It automatically recalculates the bar heights to force an even split
It removes the bars entirely and replaces them with a single flat line
It has no visible effect unless probabilities are already exactly 0.5 and 0.5
questions.explain: axhline draws a full-width horizontal line at a given y-value as a visual reference; placed at N/2, it makes the skew of a non-even distribution immediately visible by contrast, which is exactly its purpose here.

questions.q: Using the lesson's `plot_expected_counts` function with `probabilities=[0.1, 0.9]` and `n_shots=500`, what expected counts does it compute?
options: 10 and 90
questions.explain: The function computes n_shots * p for each probability: 500 * 0.1 = 50 and 500 * 0.9 = 450.
